paragraphs: AnimeSR addresses the restoration of low-quality animation videos at higher resolution. Its starting point is that training data must reflect the damage found in actual videos. Existing approaches commonly simulate degradation with fixed blur, noise, and compression operations. The paper instead learns basic degradation operators from real low-quality animation footage and incorporates them into the simulation pipeline.

These learned operators could capture real degradation patterns more faithfully, giving the restoration model more relevant examples to learn from. The work also introduces AVC, a large collection of high-quality animation videos for training and evaluation. Together, the learned degradation process and the dataset address how to construct useful training material for animation super-resolution.

The third contribution is an efficient network with multiple processing scales. It combines advantages of unidirectional recurrent processing and sliding-window methods. The authors report that the resulting AnimeSR system restores real-world animation effectively and efficiently, outperforming previous leading methods. The contribution therefore spans training-data construction, evaluation resources, and model design.
neurips-2022-animesr-learning-real-world.tldr: AnimeSR combines learned video degradations, a high-quality animation dataset, and an efficient network to improve real-world animation super-resolution.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether very strong Go agents can make obvious mistakes after changes that leave a position's strategic meaning intact. The authors define adversarial positions by adding meaningless moves to an existing game state. A successful attack makes the agent choose a clearly inferior action, rather than merely changing its preferred move.

Finding such positions is difficult because the search space is enormous, discrete, and unsuitable for direct differentiation. The proposed attack strategically narrows that space to locate adversarial states efficiently. Experiments show that adding one or two meaningless stones can mislead both the policy-value neural network and decisions made using Monte Carlo tree search.

In the reported setting, adding two stones caused KataGo with 50 search simulations to choose a losing action on 58% of AlphaGo Zero self-play games. Amateur human evaluations judged 90% of the discovered examples to induce obviously inferior play. These findings show that strong playing performance can coexist with sensitivity to strategically irrelevant changes; the method also extends to NoGo.
neurips-2022-are-alphazero-like-agents-r.tldr: Strategically meaningless stones can induce obvious mistakes in strong Go agents, including agents that use tree search.

paragraphs: When an automated assessment rule is secret, people seeking better decisions must choose changes to their observable features with incomplete information. This paper models guidance in that setting as Bayesian persuasion. The decision maker sends an action recommendation designed to encourage desirable changes while accounting for the person's incentives to follow it.

Within the model, using persuasion leaves both parties no worse off in expectation, and can substantially benefit the decision maker. The expectation qualification matters: the result concerns expected outcomes rather than a promise about every individual outcome. The central computational problem is finding the best signaling policy that remains compatible with the recipient's incentives.

Initially, that optimization involves infinitely many variables. The authors reformulate it as a linear program over finitely many regions of possible assessment rules. Even this representation can require exponentially many variables, motivating a polynomial-time approximation scheme for a near-optimal policy. Simulations on semi-synthetic data provide empirical support for the benefits of persuasion in algorithmic recourse.
neurips-2022-bayesian-persuasion-for-alg.tldr: Bayesian persuasion provides incentive-compatible recourse recommendations under secret assessment rules, with expected benefits and an efficient approximation scheme.

paragraphs: Privacy-preserving analysis often starts with a privacy budget and asks how accurate an answer can be. This paper studies the reverse priority: obtain sufficiently accurate results while retaining as much privacy as possible. It builds on noise reduction, where correlated noisy releases let a practitioner progressively improve an estimate instead of committing to its accuracy upfront.

The proposed Brownian mechanism extends this idea to Gaussian noise. It starts with a highly noisy estimate associated with the endpoint of a simulated Brownian motion. When greater accuracy is needed, it traces that same path backward to an earlier time, reducing the noise. Linking the releases through one path supports control of privacy loss across the interaction.

The mechanism fits settings with bounded sensitivity measured in the l2 norm and empirically outperforms existing work on common statistical tasks. The authors also introduce ReducedAboveThreshold, which supplies adaptive privacy guarantees. Together, these contributions support accuracy-driven analysis with customizable privacy accounting, and demonstrate that meeting utility requirements can remain compatible with strong privacy protection.
neurips-2022-brownian-noise-reduction-ma.tldr: The Brownian mechanism progressively reduces correlated Gaussian noise to support accuracy targets while controlling privacy loss.

paragraphs: Estimating causal effects from observational data often assumes that all confounding variables have been measured. Proximal inference offers an alternative when some confounders remain hidden, provided sufficiently rich proxy measurements satisfy particular structural conditions. This paper develops a neural-network approach to estimation within that framework, retaining the importance of those proxy requirements.

The computational challenge is estimating a bridge function by solving an ill-posed integral equation. Earlier methods often rely on kernel functions selected in advance. The abstract identifies two drawbacks of that approach: those kernels do not adapt to the data, and the resulting methods can struggle with large datasets. The proposed deep-learning method aims to make bridge estimation more flexible and scalable.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance on two established proximal-inference benchmarks and provide theoretical consistency guarantees. The contribution combines an estimation method with empirical and theoretical support. Its significance is making a proxy-based route to causal estimation more practical when unmeasured confounding is present and the required identification conditions hold.
neurips-2022-deep-learning-methods-for-p.tldr: A neural approach makes proximal causal inference more flexible and scalable while retaining proxy-based assumptions and consistency guarantees.

paragraphs: A predictor that satisfies a statistical fairness criterion on one population may behave differently after deployment conditions change. This paper asks how much fairness can deteriorate when the target distribution is unknown but its difference from the source distribution is bounded. The setting covers classifiers and regressors, including changes arising from uncertain training data, user adaptation, or new deployment environments.

The main contribution is a general upper bound on fairness violations after such a shift. Rather than treating fairness on the source population as sufficient evidence for deployment, the framework connects possible violations to the permitted distribution change. The authors then derive specific bounds for demographic parity and equalized odds under covariate shift and label shift.

The bounds are compared with deterministic shift models and real-world data. The authors find that useful fairness-violation bounds can be estimated in practice even when simplifying assumptions hold only approximately. These results provide a way to flag potentially inappropriate deployments, with conclusions tied to the fairness definition and the restrictions placed on distribution shift.
neurips-2022-fairness-transferability-su.tldr: The paper bounds how much statistical group fairness can deteriorate under bounded changes in the deployment distribution.

paragraphs: GenerSpeech tackles text-to-speech generation using a reference recording whose speaking style was unseen during training. Style includes speaker identity, emotion, and prosody, so successful transfer must capture both broad vocal characteristics and fine variations within speech. The challenge is to reproduce those characteristics while handling conditions that differ from the training data.

The model separates variation associated with linguistic content from variation associated with style. A multilevel style adaptor represents global speaker and emotion characteristics alongside finer prosodic information at utterance, word, and phoneme scales. A separate content adaptor uses Mix-Style Layer Normalization to remove style information from the content representation, helping it generalize across different speaking conditions.

In zero-shot style-transfer evaluations, the authors report better audio quality and style similarity than the state-of-the-art models they compare against. Additional adaptation studies report robust performance when only a few examples are available. The findings support combining detailed style modeling with a content representation designed to avoid carrying style information.
neurips-2022-generspeech-towards-style-t.tldr: GenerSpeech separates content from multilevel vocal style to improve speech synthesis with unseen reference styles and few-shot adaptation.

paragraphs: Partially monotone regression requires predictions to increase monotonically with respect to selected input features. This makes the direction of those feature effects a constraint on the model. The paper focuses on lattice layers, a core component of TensorFlow Lattice, and asks how to preserve these constraints while making training and input handling more practical.

Conventional lattice layers present two problems highlighted in the abstract. Training requires projected gradient descent with many constraints, and memory consumption prevents the layer from accepting high-dimensional input vectors. The proposed hierarchical lattice layer extends the original construction to address both issues. It supports standard stochastic gradient descent while satisfying monotonicity constraints and can receive high-dimensional inputs.

Experiments on real datasets show that these changes did not sacrifice predictive performance relative to the lattice layer. The reported contribution is therefore a more usable way to build partially monotone neural networks: the required directional behavior is maintained while the training procedure and dimensionality restrictions are improved.
neurips-2022-hierarchical-lattice-layer-.tldr: Hierarchical lattice layers preserve monotonicity while supporting standard stochastic training and high-dimensional inputs without reported predictive losses.

paragraphs: Self-supervised learning can produce useful representations, but empirical success alone does not explain which representation properties make later prediction tasks easy. This paper approaches that question through an idealized target: representations on which a trained prediction head, such as a linear model or multilayer perceptron, can achieve perfect accuracy.

The authors prove necessary and sufficient conditions for this target across tasks that remain unchanged under specified data augmentations. That restriction is central to the result: the characterization concerns tasks invariant to the chosen transformations. The conditions provide a common framework for understanding and improving both contrastive and non-contrastive approaches to self-supervised learning.

For contrastive methods, the framework motivates changes including asymmetric projection heads. For non-contrastive methods, it leads to a new, simple training objective. The resulting algorithms outperform baselines on standard benchmarks, including SwAV with multiple crops in ImageNet linear probing. The paper thus connects a conditional mathematical characterization of ideal representations to practical changes with measured downstream benefits.
neurips-2022-improving-self-supervised-l.tldr: A characterization of ideal representations yields improvements to contrastive and non-contrastive self-supervised learning with benchmark gains.

paragraphs: Gradient-boosted regression trees are widely used for tabular prediction, but a point estimate alone does not express uncertainty. IBUG extends any such point predictor to produce a distribution around its prediction. It uses nearby training examples to construct that distribution without requiring a fixed parametric distributional form.

The key choice is how to identify nearby examples. IBUG measures similarity with a tree-ensemble kernel and selects the k nearest training instances. This makes the neighborhood depend on the ensemble's representation of the data. Its runtime depends on how many training examples occupy the ensemble's leaves; sampling trees or examples can reduce that computational burden.

Across 22 benchmark regression datasets, IBUG achieves similar or better performance than the previous state of the art. Different base tree models can further improve probabilistic performance, and the method offers greater distributional flexibility than competitors. The authors also observe poor calibration in previous methods on some datasets and show that a scalar adjustment tuned on validation data can mitigate it.
neurips-2022-instance-based-uncertainty-.tldr: IBUG turns boosted-tree point predictions into flexible uncertainty distributions using nearby training examples identified through the tree ensemble.

paragraphs: This paper studies contextual linear bandits when the agents making decisions are geographically separated from the central learner. Agents observe the contexts and take actions, while the learner performs learning without seeing those contexts. Communicating high-dimensional contextual information can become a bottleneck, particularly in wireless settings, so the goal is to reduce that communication without substantially worsening learning performance.

The analysis assumes contexts come from a distribution and distinguishes whether that distribution is known. When it is unknown, the proposed method uses approximately five times the context dimension in bits per context. When it is known, the method requires zero bits per context. Both cases achieve nearly the regret bound available when contexts are directly observable.

For the unknown-distribution case, the communication bound improves on existing bounds by a logarithmic factor in the time horizon. For the known-distribution case, the authors establish information-theoretic tightness. These results identify how distributional knowledge can reduce context communication while preserving nearly the same decision-learning guarantee.
neurips-2022-learning-from-distributed-u.tldr: Distributed contextual bandits can nearly match full-context regret using about 5d bits per context, or none when its distribution is known.

paragraphs: Congestion games describe interactions in which multiple players use shared facilities and their choices affect one another. This paper studies learning in these games with limited feedback, focusing on Nash regret. A central difficulty is that the available actions can form an exponentially large set even when the number of facilities is relatively modest.

The authors develop two algorithms that exploit the game's structure. A centralized algorithm follows the principle of optimism under uncertainty and supports bandit or semi-bandit feedback, with finite-sample guarantees. A decentralized algorithm combines the Frank-Wolfe optimization method with G-optimal design. For both, sample complexity depends polynomially on player and facility counts rather than on the action-set size.

The paper also introduces Markov congestion games to represent non-stationarity in congestion settings. Its centralized algorithm for this extension again has polynomial sample complexity in the relevant problem parameters without depending on action-set size. The shared contribution is a way to obtain learning guarantees that avoid scaling with the potentially enormous collection of actions.
neurips-2022-learning-in-congestion-game.tldr: Structure-aware algorithms learn in congestion games with sample guarantees that avoid dependence on exponentially large action sets.

paragraphs: LOG addresses adaptation to distributions that differ from the training data while keeping labeling costs relatively small. The objective includes worst-case generalization across a variety of distributions, rather than performance on just one favorable target. The paper motivates this problem through open-world settings where observations need not follow a single independent, identically distributed source.

The framework combines active sample selection with causal invariant learning. Its sample-selection component searches for examples that violate the invariant relationship currently used by the model. The authors formulate this selection task as separating a mixture distribution and provide an unbiased estimator with a provable guarantee. Labeling informative violations can then support refinement of the learned invariant relationship.

The theoretical analysis supports contributions from both modules to generalization and shows how active adaptation can combine performance with robustness through invariant risk minimization. Extensive experiments report promising performance for the resulting algorithm. The contribution is an interactive approach in which selecting what to label and learning stable relationships work together toward label-efficient generalization.
neurips-2022-log-active-model-adaptation.tldr: LOG combines targeted labeling of invariant-relationship violations with causal invariant learning to improve label-efficient out-of-distribution adaptation.

paragraphs: Better accuracy on familiar data often comes with a predictable improvement on shifted data. This paper examines the rarer models that exceed that relationship, described as effectively robust. It asks which properties of models and shifted datasets help explain that extra robustness, rather than merely explaining strong overall accuracy.

The authors conduct an empirical study across natural and synthetic shifts of CIFAR-10 and ImageNet. They examine approaches associated with robustness, including pruning, augmentation, and the use of large pretrained models. Their central perspective is spectral: they investigate how Fourier properties of the models and data correlate with performance under distribution shift.

This perspective provides some insight into the robustness of certain models, especially members of the CLIP family. However, the study finds that no known metric consistently offers the best explanation. To support further investigation, the authors release RobustNets, pretrained CIFAR-10 models spanning different levels of out-of-distribution robustness. The work supplies both partial explanatory evidence and a model collection for studying the remaining puzzle.
neurips-2022-models-out-of-line-a-fourie.tldr: Fourier analysis partly explains exceptional distribution-shift robustness, but no examined metric consistently explains it best.

paragraphs: This paper develops privacy-preserving algorithms for empirical risk minimization with smooth, nonconvex objectives. Its optimization guarantee concerns finding a point with a small gradient norm. That is the quantity improved by the analysis, so the result describes progress toward stationarity rather than establishing that the algorithm finds a globally best solution.

The main technical contribution is a refined sensitivity analysis of stochastic gradient descent. It explicitly exploits the fact that training examples recur across epochs. The authors combine this analysis with results on momentum and private aggregation to obtain an algorithm satisfying epsilon-delta differential privacy. These ingredients connect the effect of individual examples to the privacy and convergence analysis.

For dimension d and sample count N, the reported gradient-norm bound is O(d^(1/3)/(epsilon N)^(2/3)), with O(N^(7/3) epsilon^(4/3)/d^(2/3)) gradient evaluations. The authors present this as an improvement over the previous best bound, approximately d^(1/4)/sqrt(epsilon N), up to logarithmic factors. The result makes the dependence on dimension, data quantity, privacy, and computational work explicit.
neurips-2022-momentum-aggregation-for-pr.tldr: A sensitivity analysis exploiting repeated examples, combined with momentum and private aggregation, improves private nonconvex optimization guarantees.

paragraphs: Adaptive step sizes can reduce the need for problem-specific tuning in ordinary optimization, but minimax problems involve coordinating minimization and maximization. This paper shows that simply adding adaptive steps to gradient descent-ascent can diverge when the ratio between the two step sizes is poorly chosen. Adaptivity alone therefore does not provide the desired freedom from parameter tuning.

NeAda addresses this coordination problem with nested loops. An inner loop adaptively maximizes over the dual variable until a controllable stopping criterion is met. An outer loop adaptively minimizes over the primal variable. The framework accepts existing adaptive optimizers and uses this structure to balance progress between the two variables.

For nonconvex-strongly-concave problems, NeAda with AdaGrad steps achieves near-optimal gradient complexities of approximately epsilon^(-2) in deterministic settings and epsilon^(-4) in stochastic settings, suppressing logarithmic factors. These guarantees do not require advance knowledge of smoothness or strong-concavity parameters. Experiments on test functions and a real-world application further illustrate robustness, connecting the theoretical coordination mechanism to practical optimization behavior.
neurips-2022-nest-your-adaptive-algorith.tldr: NeAda nests adaptive maximization inside minimization to obtain parameter-agnostic, near-optimal guarantees for nonconvex-strongly-concave minimax problems.

paragraphs: This paper studies operations on scalar and vector fields defined over a manifold. It asks which operations commute with every diffeomorphism, meaning that transforming the field and then applying the operation gives the same result as performing those steps in reverse order. This is a demanding symmetry requirement with consequences for geometric neural-network design.

For the scalar-field spaces considered, the authors prove that the qualifying operations are pointwise nonlinearities. Each output value is determined at its own location. The result extends known findings in Euclidean space and explains why these nonlinearities form a universal family compatible with arbitrary symmetry groups. It supports combining them with linear operators tailored to particular symmetries.

The vector-field result is much more restrictive: only scalar multiplication survives the full diffeomorphism requirement. Consequently, this symmetry group does not yield a universal class of nonlinear vector-field operators for neural-network construction. The contrast shows how the type of field changes what is possible under the same broad symmetry demand.
neurips-2022-on-non-linear-operators-for.tldr: Commuting with all diffeomorphisms permits pointwise nonlinearities for scalar fields but restricts vector-field operators to scalar multiplication.

paragraphs: Recurrent neural networks can be difficult to train because gradients propagated through time vanish or explode. Some remedies impose restrictions that stabilize recurrent behavior, but those restrictions can also eliminate multistability or chaos. That creates a problem when the purpose of learning is to reconstruct a dynamical system whose behavior is itself chaotic.

The paper connects training gradients to the Lyapunov spectrum of trajectories generated by the RNN. This spectrum characterizes the stability of the generated dynamics and provides a mathematical link between the behavior being modeled and the optimization difficulty. The authors prove that stable equilibrium or cyclic behavior has bounded gradients, whereas chaotic RNN dynamics have gradients that diverge.

The analysis exposes a tension between suppressing gradient growth and retaining the dynamics needed for chaotic data. Based on this connection, the authors suggest ways to adjust training according to the system's Lyapunov spectrum, independently of the chosen RNN architecture. The contribution is a theoretical explanation of the difficulty together with guidance informed by the dynamics being learned.
neurips-2022-on-the-difficulty-of-learni.tldr: The paper links RNN gradient divergence to chaotic dynamics through Lyapunov spectra and uses that connection to guide training.

paragraphs: This paper investigates the inductive biases of over-parameterized convolutional architectures through their Gaussian Process and Neural Tangent kernels. Its focus is how locality and hierarchical structure shape the functions represented by these kernels. A spectral description makes those architectural preferences mathematically explicit rather than leaving them as broad intuitions about convolutional networks.

Under normalized multichannel inputs, ReLU activation, and the uniform measure, the authors identify the kernels' eigenfunctions. They are products of spherical harmonics defined across the channels at different pixels. This supplies a structured family of functions in which to analyze the kernels, with the input normalization and measure forming part of the stated mathematical setting.

The authors then use hierarchical factorizable kernels to bound the corresponding eigenvalues. They prove polynomial decay, quantify its rate, and derive measures reflecting how hierarchical features are composed. Together, these results give a quantitative account of the role of locality and hierarchy in the inductive bias of the convolutional architectures studied.
neurips-2022-on-the-spectral-bias-of-con.tldr: Kernel eigenfunctions and eigenvalue bounds quantify how locality and hierarchy shape the inductive bias of over-parameterized convolutional networks.

paragraphs: LiDAR point clouds capture detailed geometry, but collecting and labeling enough of them remains difficult. PolarMix tackles this data constraint by creating additional training variation from existing scans. Its augmentations follow the scanning direction of rotating LiDAR sensors, aiming to enrich the data distribution while preserving the fidelity of the point clouds.

The method uses two ways of mixing information across scans. At the scene level, it cuts sectors along the scanning direction and exchanges them between two scans. At the instance level, it extracts object point instances, rotates them through multiple angles to create copies, and pastes those copies into other scans. These operations introduce variation at both scene and object scales.

Experiments report consistently superior performance across multiple perception tasks and scenarios. The method can be added to different 3D network architectures and also performs well in unsupervised domain adaptation. Its contribution is a broadly applicable augmentation procedure that uses the organization of LiDAR scans to make existing data more useful.
neurips-2022-polarmix-a-general-data-aug.tldr: PolarMix augments LiDAR data by swapping scan sectors and rotating and pasting object instances, improving multiple perception tasks.

paragraphs: Specifying a reward function can be difficult even when a human understands the intended task. Human feedback offers an alternative, but collecting large amounts of it is costly. This paper develops a theoretical framework for reducing the reward feedback needed to obtain a nearly optimal reinforcement-learning policy.

The algorithm first explores the environment without a specified reward function. It then actively selects state-action pairs and asks a human teacher about their rewards. Separating exploration from these targeted queries lets the method focus human input on learning the task's reward. The authors prove a high-probability guarantee for a nearly optimal policy, including when feedback contains random noise.

The stated reward-query bound is approximately H times dim_R squared, up to logarithmic factors, where H is the horizon and dim_R measures reward-function-class complexity. The guarantee supports an epsilon-optimal policy for any positive epsilon. The abstract contrasts this with standard methods whose reward-query requirements grow polynomially with transition complexity and inverse accuracy, highlighting the value of actively choosing reward questions.
neurips-2022-provably-feedback-efficient.tldr: Reward-free exploration followed by active human reward queries yields provably near-optimal policies with low feedback requirements, even under noisy feedback.

paragraphs: Transformers combine information across sequence elements, but ordinary representations must carry both local details and broader context. Processing long sequences also encounters the quadratic cost of self-attention. The Recurrent Memory Transformer introduces explicit memory that carries information between sequence segments, giving the model a way to retain context beyond an individual segment.

The mechanism uses special memory tokens added to the input or output sequence, without changing the Transformer model itself. Training teaches the model to manage memory operations alongside ordinary sequence processing. Recurrence passes that memory between segments, allowing it to store and process both local and global information across a longer sequence.

Experiments report language-modeling performance comparable to Transformer-XL with smaller memory sizes and better performance on tasks requiring longer sequence processing. Adding memory tokens to Transformer-XL also improves its performance. These findings make the approach promising for long-term dependencies and general memory processing; algorithmic tasks and reasoning are identified as potential application areas.
neurips-2022-recurrent-memory-transforme.tldr: Recurrent Memory Transformer carries learned memory tokens between segments to improve long-sequence processing without changing the Transformer model.

paragraphs: Text generation models can expose sensitive training information. SeqPATE adapts the private learning method PATE to protect individual training samples and sensitive phrases. The challenge is that generation produces a sequence of tokens from a large vocabulary, whereas classic PATE is not customized for that setting or for protecting phrases within samples.

The method generates pseudo-contexts and recasts sequence generation as next-word prediction. It dynamically filters candidate outputs to shrink the prediction space, then refines teacher aggregation to address weak agreement when votes are spread across many possible words. These changes adapt the teaching mechanism to the structure and scale of text generation.

SeqPATE also uses knowledge distillation to reduce the number of teacher queries, lowering privacy losses associated with those queries. Experiments support its effectiveness in protecting both training samples and sensitive phrases. The paper's contribution is a coordinated adaptation of context generation, candidate selection, aggregation, and distillation so that private teacher-based learning can serve sequential text models.
neurips-2022-seqpate-differentially-priv.tldr: SeqPATE adapts private teacher aggregation and distillation to text generation, protecting training samples and sensitive phrases.

paragraphs: Optical flow estimates motion between video frames, but occlusion removes the local matching evidence needed to track some regions. SKFlow addresses this difficulty by enlarging the area of information available to its convolutional network. Its super kernels provide broader receptive fields to help infer motions where direct correspondence is missing.

Large receptive fields must also be computationally practical. The authors design the super kernels using conical connections and hybrid depth-wise convolutions, aiming to gain broader context efficiently. This connects the architecture directly to the stated failure mode: insufficient local evidence in occluded areas. Experiments across multiple benchmarks report improvements, particularly in those areas.

In the reported comparison, SKFlow ranks first among then-published methods on Sintel, without an ImageNet-pretrained backbone and with a modest computational increase. On the clean and final test passes, it improves the best published unmatched-area results by 9.09% and 7.92%, respectively. These results support the usefulness of efficiently expanding context when motion matching is obstructed.
neurips-2022-skflow-learning-optical-flo.tldr: SKFlow uses efficient large convolutional kernels to improve optical-flow estimation, especially where occlusion removes local matching evidence.

paragraphs: Sentence scoring assigns a likelihood-based score to a sentence, supporting tasks such as choosing among candidate outputs. Existing language-modeling approaches face a tradeoff. Causal models estimate probabilities using context in only one direction, while masked models use bidirectional information but require multiple forward passes to score all the tokens in a sentence.

Transcormer introduces sliding language modeling to combine bidirectional context with single-pass scoring. Its triple-stream self-attention mechanism estimates probabilities for every token during one forward pass. This makes the attention design central to both goals: using information from both sides of a token and avoiding repeated model evaluations for the complete sentence.

Experiments on multiple tasks report better performance than the other language-modeling approaches considered. The stated significance is improved scoring effectiveness together with computational efficiency. By designing the training and attention mechanism specifically for sentence scoring, Transcormer addresses the limitations that arise when causal or masked language models are used for this purpose.
neurips-2022-transcormer-transformer-for.tldr: Transcormer uses triple-stream attention to score all sentence tokens with bidirectional context in a single forward pass.
